title: Tabularis Run — defeat The Deadlock
author: debba_
selftext:
I maintain Tabularis, an open-source AI-native database client. The hard part of any dev tool isn't the code, it's getting someone to care enough to click. So instead of writing another "check out my project" post, I built a little browser game and let people stumble into the project through it.

A Super Mario–style platformer, SQL-themed top to bottom. You stomp slow queries and deadlocks, collect hidden "plugins", fight database bosses (a SQLite hummingbird, a MySQL dolphin, a Postgres elephant), and every screen is written in SQL (COMMIT; on the flag, ROLLBACK when you die, BEGIN; checkpoints). 12 levels, 3 worlds.

Constraints I gave myself, which made the vibecoding loop way more fun:

\- Vanilla JS + Canvas, zero runtime dependencies. No engine, no framework.

\- No external assets at all: every sprite is procedural pixel art, all the music/SFX is generated WebAudio chiptune. Nothing downloaded, nothing in the repo but code.

The part I actually wanted to share: most of this was built experimenting with Fable (Anthropic's new model). It was genuinely good at the fiddly stuff that usually kills hobby gamedev momentum and collision edge cases, "why does the stomp register as a side-hit", procedural sprite grids, a headless smoke-test bot that plays all 12 levels to prove they're beatable. Having a model that could hold the whole tiny-engine in its head and reason about game-feel numbers (jump arcs, pit widths) changed how I worked.

It's all open source if you want to poke at how the procedural art/audio works: [github.com/TabularisDB/game](http://github.com/TabularisDB/game)

Curious what people here think: both about the game and about using a throwaway fun thing as a top-of-funnel for a serious tool.
